era_visual_canon.clothing: Men in work shirts and trousers, often covered in dust, including miners with basic work gear, hard hats, and boots. Women in practical dresses or skirts and blouses, suitable for hot desert climates. Children in simple, light clothing. Business attire for corporate and government officials of the era.
era_visual_canon.technology: Industrial mining machinery, basic automotive technology. Landline telephones, typewriters, analog gauges, and rudimentary industrial safety equipment. NO smartphones, no internet, no LEDs, no advanced digital displays or personal computers.
era_visual_canon.vehicles_machinery: Early to mid-20th century mining trucks, drills, and heavy machinery for asbestos extraction and processing. Utility vehicles, sedans, and small propeller aircraft from the 1940s-1960s. No modern SUVs or advanced construction equipment.
era_visual_canon.interiors: Simple, functional residential interiors with basic furnishings, often constructed with corrugated iron, wood, and asbestos sheeting. Dusty mine offices with desks, filing cabinets, and typewriters. Industrial mill interiors characterized by pervasive dust and rudimentary processing equipment.
era_visual_canon.forbidden_anachronisms: smartphones, LED screens, contemporary clothing (post-2000s), modern flat panels, GPS devices, advanced environmental monitoring drones, digital cameras, post-1980s vehicles, plastic water bottles, barcodes, modern corporate logos, solar panels, high-tech respirators.
era_visual_canon.materials_textures: Corrugated iron, weathered wood, raw blue asbestos fibers, reddish desert earth, pervasive fine dust, rough mining tailings. Concrete, cement sheeting (uralita), and other basic construction materials.
era_visual_canon.color_palette: exterior red earth, rust-browns, dull blues (from asbestos), weathered greys, pale corrugated iron; interior muted tones, pale walls, dusty surfaces.
era_visual_canon.scale_dimensions: A small isolated town, primarily composed of single-story and low-rise buildings. Set within a vast, open desert landscape, featuring unpaved roads and a basic airstrip.
era_visual_canon.distinctive_features: A deserted Australian mining town, characterized by its remote desert location and buildings, roads, and other infrastructure visibly constructed from blue asbestos mining waste, creating a vast and toxic forbidden zone.
era_visual_canon.demographics: Mainly European migrants, including Spanish, often working-class, composed of miners and their families. Indigenous Banjima people (traditional owners). Workers and residents often wore practical, durable clothing suitable for mining and desert life, often covered in dust.
era_visual_canon.visual_reference_availability: The canonical subject description serves as a primary visual reference. Written records describe building materials (corrugated iron, wood, asbestos sheets), landscape (red earth, dust), and conditions (dusty interiors, asbestos-covered surfaces). Photos of similar Australian mining towns from the era, or historical photos of Wittenoom if available, would corroborate these descriptions. Post-abandonment photos document the ghost town's state and current permanent barricades.

condition_evolution.at_event: A functioning, albeit dusty and hazardous, mining town with active mines, a mill, basic residences, and infrastructure. Buildings and roads are constructed using asbestos tailings.
condition_evolution.later: A deserted ghost town, formally abolished, with many buildings demolished and services disconnected. Remaining structures are derelict, weathered, and heavily contaminated by dispersed blue asbestos, with permanent blockades preventing access.

documented_props.forma: Structures, often low-rise, built from corrugated iron, wood, and asbestos sheeting or containing asbestos tailings, now derelict and abandoned.
Fibrous blue mineral material, often appearing as fine dust or integrated into construction materials and ground surfaces, dispersed widely throughout the environment.
Physical barriers such as fences, signs, and concrete structures installed at entry points to the former town and gorge to prevent human access.
